answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: Three scenarios were used: 1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category), 2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category), and 3) Current Policies (Hot House World Category).
answers.evidence:
The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios:

Scenario | Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category) | Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category) | Current Policies (Hot House World Category)

Description:
- Net Zero 2050: An ambitious and coordinated transition to a low-emissions, climate resilient future. Stringent climate policies, innovation, ambitious investment, and medium-to-high deployment of carbon removal solutions limit global warming to 1.6°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.4°C by 2100.
- Delayed Transition: Ambitious action is delayed to 2030, followed by sudden and uncoordinated economic transformation. Extensive, stringent and punitive but late government intervention, in combination with some deployment of carbon removal solutions limit global warming to 1.7°C in 2050 and reducing to 1.6°C by 2100.
- Current Policies: Current emissions reduction policies are implemented. Current socio-economic trends continue, resulting in 2°C global warming by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100.
answers.location_hint: Page 2 of Climate-Related Disclosures / Page 24 of Annual Report
answers.notes: All three scenarios are based on NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System) scenarios and are explicitly named and described in the document.

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer:
The document describes three scenarios with the following global temperature outcomes by 2100:
1. Net Zero 2050 (Orderly): 1.4°C by 2100
2. Delayed Transition (Disorderly): 1.6°C by 2100
3. Current Policies (Hot House World): more than 3°C by 2100

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. Briscoe Group collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios customised for New Zealand's retail sector, based on three NGFS scenarios: Net Zero 2050 (Orderly), Delayed Transition (Disorderly), and Current Policies (Hot House World). A retail sector narrative was formed for each scenario, and external experts were then engaged to perform a Briscoe Group-specific risk assessment through workshops with the SWG and key management.
answers.evidence: "In the first half of the year, we collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios... A retail sector narrative was formed for each scenario identifying the critical interactions and key outcomes and indicators. These scenarios considered three different time horizons: short (2023-2030), medium (2031-2040) and long (2041-2050) and explored the political, environmental, societal, technological, legal and economic impacts across each potential pathway. We then engaged external experts to assist us in interrogating these scenarios and performing a Briscoe Group specific risk assessment."
answers.location_hint: Annual Report p.24–25; Climate-Related Disclosures p.2–3
answers.notes: The scenarios are sector-level customisations built on NGFS frameworks, tailored for New Zealand's retail sector, and then further applied at the Briscoe Group entity level through workshops.

answers.answer: The baseline scenario represents 1.1°C of global warming, helping to identify the current physical and transition impacts incurred. The three NGFS-based scenarios used are: (1) Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Category) – limiting warming to 1.6°C in 2050; (2) Delayed Transition (Disorderly Category) – limiting warming to 1.7°C in 2050; and (3) Current Policies (Hot House World Category) – resulting in 2°C by 2050 and more than 3°C by 2100.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. Briscoe Group considers damage from acute physical risks including: increased storminess/extreme winds, river and pluvial flooding, and global supply chain disruption from storms/floods. These are identified as key physical risks with potential impacts including store closures, supply chain delays, cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings, increased lease costs, and loss of sales/profit.
answers.evidence: "Increased storminess/ extreme winds / River and pluvial flooding: Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency. There will be an increasing incidence of storm events with increasing severity impacting supply chains and operations. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Team and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Climate-Related Disclosures, pages 3-4; Annual Report pages 25-26
answers.notes: Acute physical risks explicitly considered include increased storminess/extreme winds, river and pluvial flooding, and global supply chain disruption from storms/floods affecting international ports. Sea-level rise (a chronic risk) is also discussed separately.

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group uses three time horizons for climate-related risk assessment at the entity level:
- Short-term: one to three years
- Medium-term: three to 10 years
- Long-term: more than 10 years

For scenario analysis, the sector-based time horizons used were: short (2023–2030), medium (2031–2040), and long (2041–2050).
answers.evidence: "The time horizons utilised in the climate-risk assessment process were: • Short-term: one to three years • Medium-term: three to 10 years • Long term: > 10years" and "These scenarios considered three different time horizons: short (2023-2030), medium (2031-2040) and long (2041-2050)"
answers.location_hint: Climate-Related Disclosures, Risk Management section (p.5); Strategy section (p.2/p.24 of Annual Report)
answers.notes: Two sets of time horizons are defined: sector-level scenario horizons (2023–2050) and entity-level business planning horizons (1–3 years, 3–10 years, >10 years). Note also that Adoption Provision 2 exempts the company from disclosing the time horizons over which anticipated financial impacts could reasonably be expected to occur.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: Briscoe Group, in collaboration with other retail industry participants, chose three NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System) scenarios adapted into retail sector narratives. The justification for using a combination of scenarios was to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy, as they prepare for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term. The three scenarios (Net Zero 2050/Orderly, Delayed Transition/Disorderly, and Current Policies/Hothouse World) were chosen to cover a range of physical and transition impacts: from lowest physical impacts with moderate transition impacts (Orderly), to moderate physical with highest transition impacts (Disorderly), to highest physical impacts with lowest transition impacts (Hothouse World). The scenarios were also aligned to entity-level business planning and investment timeframes.
answers.evidence: "In the first half of the year, we collaborated with other retail industry participants to co-design a set of integrated climate change scenarios for New Zealand's retail sector. The sector group chose the following three Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios as the basis for the sector-level scenarios... Using a combination of scenarios was intended to add resilience to the risk assessment process and the resultant strategy as we prepare for inevitable uncertainty in the short to medium-term."
answers.location_hint: Briscoe Group 2024 Annual Report, p.24; Climate-Related Disclosures, p.3
answers.notes: The document explicitly states the rationale for using a combination of scenarios (resilience to uncertainty) and identifies the NGFS framework as the basis. The scenarios cover orderly, disorderly, and hothouse world pathways to ensure a comprehensive range of physical and transition risk outcomes are assessed.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: Briscoe Group has experienced some historic climate impacts, though physical impacts have not significantly impacted operations. These include: (1) transitional impacts such as increased legislation (specifically the newly introduced NZ Climate related disclosures) and an increase in insurance premiums off the back of climate-related events occurring in NZ; (2) some team members, particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland, felt the impacts of severe weather events earlier in the year. The company has not identified any material impacts requiring specific disclosure in the financial statements.
answers.evidence: "Although we have started to feel the transitional impacts of climate change on our business relating to increased legislation (specifically the newly introduced NZ Climate related disclosures) and have seen an increase in insurance premiums off the back of climate-related events occurring in NZ, we have been fortunate that the physical impacts experienced by our business have not significantly impacted operations. We are cognisant some of our team members particularly in Hastings, Napier, Gisborne and parts of Auckland felt the impacts of the severe weather events earlier in the year..."
answers.location_hint: Strategy section, Annual Report p.24 / Climate-Related Disclosures p.2
answers.notes: The document also notes in the financial statements that "we have not identified any material impacts requiring specific disclosure in the financial statements."

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer:
Briscoe Group identifies the following key physical climate risks:

1. **Sustainable Sourcing (indirect):** Climate-related events increasing globally impact the availability of raw materials for suppliers, affecting product availability, increasing inventory costs, and decreasing margins/profit. Business response: diversification of product range and working with suppliers to ensure diversity and sustainable sourcing.

2. **Increased storminess / extreme winds / river and pluvial flooding (direct):** Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones, changes in extreme wind speed, convective weather events, high-intensity rainfall, and hail severity. Impacts include potential store closures, supply chain delays, inability of team and customers to reach stores, loss of sales, cost of repairs/maintenance, increased lease costs, and increased supply chain costs. Business response: transition planning to ensure resilience to extreme weather events.

3. **Global supply chain risk (indirect):** A main international port affected by storms or floods, leading to inability to get goods to New Zealand, need to source from alternative locations, and supply chain delays. Financial impact: loss of sales, decreased profit, increased supply chain costs. Business response: transition planning to build resilience into supply chain.

4. **Sea-level rise leading to coastal and estuarine flooding (direct):** Relative sea-level rise (including land movement), change in tidal range, permanent increase in spring high-tide inundation, rising groundwater. Sea level rise of 0.32m could impact specific locations and increase losses due to flooding, potential store closures, supply chain delays, and inability of team/customers to reach stores. Financial impact: loss of sales, cost of repairs/maintenance, increased lease costs, increased supply chain costs. Business response: work underway to identify at-risk catchments and transition planning to mitigate risk.
answers.evidence:
"KEY PHYSICAL RISKS: Sustainable Sourcing – With climate-related events increasing globally, this is a significant risk to those who want to source sustainable products. Impact of a changing climate on the availability of raw materials for our suppliers. Availability of products offered to us from our suppliers. Decreased ability to purchase required levels of inventory. Increased cost of inventory. Decrease in margin/profit. Working with suppliers to ensure diversity in product ranges and that products are sourced sustainably.

Increased storminess/extreme winds / River and pluvial flooding – Increase in storminess (frequency, intensity) including tropical cyclones. Changes in extreme wind speed. Increase in convective weather events (tornadoes, lightning). Changes in extremes: high intensity and persistence of rainfall. Increase in hail severity or frequency. There will be an increasing incidence of storm events with increasing severity impacting supply chains and operations. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Team and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs. Transition planning to ensure resilience to extreme weather events.

Global supply chain risk – A main international port is affected (e.g. by storms/or floods). Unable to get goods to New Zealand. Need to source goods from alternative location. Delays in supply chain. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Increased supply chain costs. Transition planning to build resilience into supply chain.

Sea-level rise leading to coastal and estuarine flooding – Relative sea-level rise (including land movement). Change in tidal range or increased water depth. Permanent increase in spring high-tide inundation. Rising groundwater from sea-level rise. Sea level rise of 0.32m could impact specific locations and increase losses due to flooding. Potential store closures. Delays in supply chain. Team and customers unable to get to our stores. Loss of sales and decrease in profit. Cost of repairs/maintenance to buildings. Increased lease costs. Increased supply chain costs. Work under way to identify at risk catchments. Transition planning to mitigate risk."
